title: How License Plates Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history of license plates, starting with the French origins under Paris police prefect Louis Lépine around 1893 and New York's 1901 initials requirement, then Massachusetts and Philadelphia's 1903 issuance, state slogans and designs (Idaho potatoes, Maine "Vacationland", Florida grapefruit/bomb plate, Ohio airplane error), the John R. Wald Company die supply, Germany's FE-Schrift created to thwart Red Army Faction forgeries, state fees, vanity and specialty plates and free speech court cases, whiskey (W) plates for DUI revocations, prison labor in plate manufacturing, embossed versus flat plates, digital plates, plate collecting and record sales, and 3M reflective sheeting. The episode also includes listener mail about cultural appropriation following the Mariachi episode.

segments.title: Opening banter and tour announcement
segments.summary: Hosts announce live shows returning in February (San Francisco, Seattle, Portland), chat about Emily's business closing, TV shows like Larry Sanders, Ju-On, and The Bear, and introduce the license plate topic as a listener request from Tracy.

segments.title: Origins of license plates in France and New York
segments.summary: Chuck guesses the US, but the French preceded it; Paris police prefect Louis Lépine regulated cars. New York in 1901 required owners' initials three inches tall, allowing customized designs, and the 1903 numbering was introduced because initials duplicated.

segments.title: 1903 issuance and first state programs
segments.summary: Philadelphia was the first US city to issue official plates; Massachusetts ran the first statewide program, numbering from one, and Frederick Tudor received number one.

segments.title: Slogans, designs, and errors
segments.summary: Covers Idaho's potato plate, Maine's Vacationland slogan since 1936, Florida's grapefruit plate that resembled a bomb, Ohio's backwards airplane error, standardized sizing in 1957, and 3M reflective sheeting in 1971.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Ad break with a host-read sponsor segment.

segments.title: Font uniformity and the German FE-Schrift
segments.summary: Plate fonts look alike largely because John R. Wald Company supplied embossing dies. Germany's DIN 1451 font was easy to forge, so the Red Army Faction exploited it; designer Carl Georg Hoefer created FE-Schrift in 1978 with serifs (seraphs) added to hinder forgery. It was later adopted for European plates.

segments.title: Fees, specialty plates, and vanity plates
segments.summary: State fees vary, from about ten dollars in Virginia to around one hundred in Washington DC for specialty plates. Specialty plates support causes and museums, and vanity plates cost more. Vanity plate rates by percentage are highest in Virginia and lowest in Texas, with Canadian provinces also compared.

segments.title: Free speech and offensive vanity plate requests
segments.summary: Discusses First Amendment issues with state-issued vanity plates, including a North Carolina white power plate and a New Hampshire or Vermont case where a Supreme Court ruling favored the state over a plate reading a dirty acronym. Some states avoid the letters O and zero to block profanity.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Ad break with a host-read sponsor segment.

segments.title: Whiskey plates, no-plate confusion, and prison-made plates
segments.summary: W 'whiskey' plates signal DUI license revocation in Minnesota and Ohio. A man who requested 'no plates' got tickets. The rumor that prison inmates make license plates is confirmed as true, with prison labor often used by contractors.

segments.title: Embossed versus flat plates, digital plates, and plate collecting
segments.summary: Vermont is the only state with depressed (debossed) lettering; roughly half of states still emboss. Digital plates are emerging in Silicon Valley-backed products. Collectors pay large sums for low tag numbers, notably in Delaware and abroad, including a New York plate sold with a Volvo.

segments.title: 3M lobbying and closing remarks on plates
segments.summary: Hosts note that 3M lobbies for more frequent plate replacement to win contracts for reflective sheeting, and wrap up the plate topic.

segments.title: Listener mail on Mariachi cultural appropriation
segments.summary: Listeners from Mexico and Mexican American communities respond to the Mariachi episode, encouraging Chuck to wear a charro suit. Listeners Joel Hernandez and Jamie Cavazos are read.
